network.overall_strategy: This connected network contains 21 molecule nodes, 12 reaction nodes, and 10 graph-distinct pathways. The pathways represent three chemical families—Strecker aminonitrile hydrolysis, hydantoin-mediated conversion, and glyoxylate/oxime reduction—not ten independently demonstrated mechanisms. Four pathways begin with externally supplied formaldehyde, four include its photochemical production from HCN, and two use supplied or photochemically generated glyoxylic acid. Molecules designated as intermediates may also enter through these explicitly identified feedstock boundaries. The strongest core is conventional aminonitrile formation and hydrolysis. Hydantoin processing and transferable photochemical glyoxylate production remain conditional extensions, identified in their reaction records. Operating windows are proposed implementation conditions unless explicitly identified as literature conditions; they are not claims of demonstrated integrated yields. Irradiated, ammonia-rich, acidic-hydrolysis, and strongly alkaline compartments are separate. No oxygen is required, and metallic iron is explicitly consumed rather than treated as an inexhaustible catalyst. The review's peracetic-acid amination, formaldehyde-to-glycolate Cannizzaro assignment, threonine-to-ethylene-oxide mechanism, and asparagine-to-two-glycine hydrolysis are not adopted because their stated mechanisms do not establish those productive conversions. Glyoxylic-acid hydration is not counted as an independent synthesis route. Neutral organic formulas are acid-reference representations of aqueous speciation; explicit redox ions retain their charges. Because the schema permits only one environment_formed value, that field records a representative formation environment, while reaction records specify all formation settings. Terminal coproducts use the available intermediate role.

reactions.name: Cyanosulfidic photoreduction supplying formaldehyde

conditions.other: Anoxic irradiated pool; proposed pH 7-9, 10-100 mM total cyanide, and submillimolar dissolved copper. Sulfide must be supplied without quantitatively precipitating the copper catalyst. A 254 nm source is a laboratory reference, not an assumed equivalent of the solar spectrum. Residence is controlled by measured formaldehyde production over hours to days. Transfer into a shaded trapping zone must compete with further homologation, photodestruction, and volatilization.

reactions.mechanism: Photoredox reduction of HCN gives a methanimine-level intermediate, whose hydrolysis supplies formaldehyde and ammonia. Sulfide supplies reducing equivalents. Idealized elemental-sulfur-limit bookkeeping is: 8 HCN + 8 H2S + 8 H2O -> 8 CH2O + 8 NH3 + S8. This is a coarse-grained reaction, not a claim that eight HCN molecules react in one elementary event.
reactions.reasoning: HCN reductive homologation using sulfide and copper photochemistry is supported by Patel et al. (2015). Copper is included for its photoredox function, not as an arbitrary mineral decoration. The proposed operating ranges and physical transfer are implementation assumptions. Actual oxidized sulfur can partition among elemental sulfur, polysulfides, and cyanide-containing sulfur products; representing its terminal elemental fraction as S8 is an idealization that requires sulfur-balance verification. Productive formaldehyde interception and persistence of dissolved copper are key bottlenecks.

reactions.name: Ammonia-first Strecker formation of aminoacetonitrile

conditions.other: Shaded, anoxic aqueous compartment; proposed pH 8-9.5, millimolar to tens-of-millimolar carbon substrates, and a molar excess of total ammonia. Assess conversion over hours to several days. Ammonia-rich conditions are established before or during cyanide addition. Covered pores or channels limit HCN and NH3 loss. This compartment is not simultaneously operated under the acidic conditions of nitrile hydrolysis.

reactions.mechanism: Formaldehyde and ammonia reversibly form a carbinolamine and methanimine/iminium pool. Cyanide addition to the imine carbon forms aminoacetonitrile. Net: CH2O + NH3 + HCN -> NH2CH2CN + H2O.
reactions.reasoning: This is conventional Strecker chemistry and is consistent with the aminonitrile chemistry discussed by Patel et al. (2015). No mineral catalyst is required. Cyanohydrin formation, formaldehyde-ammonia oligomerization, and aminonitrile side reactions compete. The operating window is proposed rather than attributed as an exact protocol from that paper. The alternative cyanohydrin branch below resolves a real reservoir within the same reaction family, not an independent experimental demonstration.

reactions.name: Formaldehyde trapping as glycolonitrile

conditions.other: Proposed pH 7-9; millimolar or greater total formaldehyde and cyanide; lower ammonia activity than in rxn_002. Use a shaded aqueous capture compartment downstream of photochemistry when rxn_001 supplies the aldehyde. Equilibration may occur over minutes to hours, but the useful reservoir fraction must be measured in the actual mixture.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to formaldehyde and the resulting alkoxide is protonated, yielding the cyanohydrin glycolonitrile. Net: CH2O + HCN -> HOCH2CN. Formation is reversible.
reactions.reasoning: Formaldehyde cyanohydrin chemistry is a chemically established part of HCN-based prebiotic networks, including the context of Patel et al. (2015). This node is justified because glycolonitrile can constitute a substantial carbon reservoir. It is not assumed to improve survival or yield automatically: reversible dissociation, hydrolysis, and photochemical consumption determine whether it can subsequently feed aminonitrile formation.

reactions.name: Ammonia-driven exchange of the glycolonitrile reservoir into aminoacetonitrile

conditions.other: Raise total ammonia activity relative to the glycolonitrile-capture stage while maintaining proposed pH 8-9.5. Keep the solution shaded and retain volatile HCN. Follow reservoir exchange over hours to days; the ammonia concentration and residence time must be sufficient to obtain a measurable aminonitrile fraction before destructive side reactions dominate.

reactions.mechanism: Glycolonitrile reversibly releases formaldehyde and cyanide; ammonia accesses the imine pool, and cyanide trapping gives aminoacetonitrile. Net: HOCH2CN + NH3 -> NH2CH2CN + H2O. This net exchange does not require a direct, uncatalyzed displacement of hydroxide from a saturated carbon.
reactions.reasoning: This is a reservoir-resolved representation of Strecker chemistry consistent with Patel et al. (2015), not evidence for a separate elementary substitution mechanism. Productive exchange depends on cyanohydrin dissociation and imine trapping in the actual mixture. The sequential ammonia change is chemically motivated and explicitly specified; neither transport nor improved yield is assumed to have been demonstrated.

reactions.name: Acid-promoted aminoacetonitrile hydration to glycinamide

conditions.other: Separate acidic geothermal pool or sheltered pore; proposed pH 0.5-1.5 and residence of days to weeks, depending on measured kinetics. Volcanic acidity need not depend on atmospheric oxygen. Transfer an aminonitrile-containing fraction from the ammonia-rich compartment only after establishing the required acidity. Keep the hydrolysis stage shielded from direct UV and prevent complete drying.

reactions.mechanism: Nitrile protonation promotes water addition, followed by proton transfers and tautomerization to the amide. Net: NH2CH2CN + H2O -> NH2CH2CONH2. The amino group will largely be protonated under these conditions, although the equation uses neutral organic reference forms.
reactions.reasoning: The aminonitrile-to-amino-acid family is supported by Patel et al. (2015); the amide is the conventional mechanistic intermediate. The supplied review's implication of efficient neutral, ambient-temperature hydrolysis is not adopted. The stated acidic, warm window is a proposed implementation rather than a reaction-specific protocol established by that paper. Hydrolysis rate, aminonitrile side reactions, and the availability of a sufficiently acidic receiving compartment remain operational constraints.

reactions.name: Glycinamide hydrolysis to glycine

conditions.other: Continue the protected aqueous hydrolysis stage at proposed pH 0.5-1.5. Evaluate conversion over days to weeks rather than assuming instant completion. Ammonia is principally ammonium in this compartment. After conversion, cooling and dilution or neutralization reduce further degradation; any subsequent concentration is physical processing rather than an additional synthesis reaction.

reactions.mechanism: Water attacks the protonated amide carbonyl. Collapse of the tetrahedral intermediate and proton transfer produce glycine and ammonia/ammonium. Neutral-reference net: NH2CH2CONH2 + H2O -> NH2CH2CO2H + NH3.
reactions.reasoning: This completes the conventional two-stage aminonitrile hydrolysis associated with the route summarized by Patel et al. (2015). The elementary amide-hydrolysis assignment is standard chemistry, but the proposed environmental residence time is not a reported yield from that study. Completion of this step, rather than merely disappearance of the nitrile, must be demonstrated. Moderate surface temperatures are chosen to avoid assuming that glycine is indefinitely stable in hotter vent fluids.

reactions.name: Carbonate-dependent Bucherer-Bergs capture of aminoacetonitrile as hydantoin

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 bar in a sheltered, gas-retaining compartment
conditions.other: Proposed pH 8.5-9.5, millimolar to tens-of-millimolar aminonitrile, and approximately 0.1-1 M total ammonium/carbonate in a locally concentrated pool. Assess cyclization over 1-3 days. NH3 and inorganic carbon belong to the molecular pools already represented in the graph. CO2 addition alone is not treated as sufficient: carbonate speciation, ammonia retention, and productive cyclization must all be established.

reactions.mechanism: Aminonitrile carbamylation is followed by intramolecular cyclization and rearrangement/hydrolytic proton-transfer steps to hydantoin. The balanced coarse-grained net is NH2CH2CN + CO2 -> hydantoin; water does not appear in the net equation.
reactions.reasoning: Bucherer-Bergs hydantoin formation is established synthetic chemistry (Bucherer and Lieb, 1934; Ware, 1950), but this branch is not demonstrated by the supplied research. Its operation in naturally concentrated carbonate waters is therefore a speculative prebiotic extension. It is included as a chemically distinct aminonitrile capture-and-conversion alternative, not as proof of improved storage. Insufficient carbonate activity, volatile loss, and diversion to other carbamylated products could prevent productive operation.

reactions.name: Alkaline hydrothermal opening of hydantoin to hydantoic acid

conditions.other: Separate alkaline subsurface geothermal fracture; proposed room-temperature-reference pH 11-12 and residence of approximately 1-3 days. High-temperature acid-base speciation must be calculated rather than equated with the room-temperature pH. This severity is a proposed test window, not an experimentally established natural-fluid protocol. Surface hydantoin must reach the hot alkaline compartment without being assumed to undergo spontaneous warm-neutral-water hydrolysis.

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxide addition at the imide carbonyl opens the hydantoin ring, yielding N-carbamoylglycinate. Neutral-reference net: hydantoin + H2O -> N-carbamoylglycine.
reactions.reasoning: Chemical opening and hydrolysis of hydantoins are documented in the hydantoin literature (Ware, 1950), but no supplied study establishes this geological implementation. It is a speculative environmental extension with an explicit severity requirement. Ring opening is shown separately because it does not by itself establish glycine production. Availability of sufficiently alkaline hot water, hydantoin residence time, and competing degradation are decisive uncertainties.

reactions.name: Hydantoic acid decarbamoylation to glycine

conditions.other: Continue or separately test the alkaline hydrothermal stage at room-temperature-reference pH 11-12 over approximately 1-4 days. Carbon dioxide is predominantly bicarbonate/carbonate under these conditions. Quantify glycine production and destruction together; promptly cool an exiting product fraction. Ring reclosure, incomplete decarbamoylation, and glycine decomposition must not be hidden by assuming quantitative conversion.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of the carbamoyl group releases glycine and an inorganic carbamate pool that decomposes to ammonia and inorganic carbon. Neutral-reference net: N-carbamoylglycine + H2O -> glycine + NH3 + CO2.
reactions.reasoning: Conversion of hydantoins through hydantoic acids to amino acids belongs to established hydantoin chemistry (Ware, 1950). Its productive operation in the proposed natural-fluid window is speculative and is not demonstrated by the supplied papers. This is the principal bottleneck of the hydantoin branch: conditions sufficient for deprotection may also destroy glycine. High-temperature decomposition studies such as Qian et al. (1993) motivate the survival constraint, but are not cited as proof of this particular conversion.

reactions.name: Conditional CO2-sulfite photoredox supply of a glyoxylic acid pool

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 bar with a replenished inorganic-carbon reservoir
conditions.other: Anoxic UV-exposed pool; proposed pH 7-9 and 10-100 mM sulfite. Use measured photon dose, with 254 nm irradiation as a laboratory reference, and assess products over hours to a day. The downstream branch is admitted only if analysis establishes an accessible glyoxylic acid/hydrate pool. Residual sulfite, sulfite adducts, and competing carbon products must be characterized before transfer into the mildly acidic hydroxylamine compartment.

reactions.mechanism: Sulfite photoionization supplies reducing equivalents for a multistep CO2-reduction and C-C-bond-forming network. The idealized glyoxylic-acid-producing net is 2 CO2 + 2 SO3(2-) + H2O -> C2H2O3 + 2 SO4(2-). This edge summarizes a possible productive branch; it is not an elementary reaction or a claim of selective conversion.
reactions.reasoning: Liu et al. (2021) support anoxic CO2/sulfite photoredox chemistry. The specific transferable glyoxylic-acid supply represented by this coarse-grained edge remains conditional: the supplied review does not establish an isolated yield or compatibility with the downstream mixture. It is therefore speculative as an integrated prebiotic supply step. Sulfite is explicitly consumed and sulfate produced, providing the required four reducing equivalents. Ordinary glyoxylic-acid hydrate dehydration is not treated as a separate photochemical synthesis.

reactions.name: Glyoxylic acid condensation with hydroxylamine

conditions.other: Shaded geothermal pool or protected aqueous pore; proposed pH 4-6, millimolar glyoxylic acid, and hydroxylamine at roughly one to several molar equivalents. Follow oxime formation over hours. For material from rxn_010, establish that sulfite adducts release accessible carbonyl substrate. Hydroxylamine is an externally supplied boundary feedstock whose sustained natural abundance is unresolved.

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxylamine adds to the aldehyde carbonyl, followed by dehydration to a hydroxyiminoacetic-acid pool. Net: OHC-CO2H + NH2OH -> HON=CH-CO2H + H2O. E/Z oxime geometry is not specified.
reactions.reasoning: Muchowska et al. (2019) support the combined hydroxylamine/metallic-iron conversion of keto-acid precursors to amino acids. Resolving oxime formation as a separate node is a mechanistic decomposition of that chemistry, not an additional independent experimental demonstration. The surface geothermal setting accommodates the reported mild temperature without forcing a 343 K experiment into a hotter vent category. Glyoxylate hydration, sulfite binding, and hydroxylamine availability constrain productive operation.

reactions.name: Stoichiometric metallic-iron reduction of glyoxylic acid oxime
agents: Reactive metallic iron surface; stoichiometric reductant, not a catalyst

conditions.other: Anoxic, shaded aqueous compartment; proposed maintained pH 4-6. At least two stoichiometric equivalents of accessible Fe(0) are required by electron balance, with additional consumption possible through corrosion and hydrogen evolution. Evaluate conversion over hours to approximately one day. Native or meteoritic iron is a conditional local resource, not assumed ubiquitous. Limit sulfide carryover and monitor passivation, iron dissolution, and competing carbonyl reduction.

reactions.mechanism: Oxime reduction requires four electrons overall, including N-O bond cleavage and reduction of the C=N functionality. Two Fe(0) atoms oxidized to Fe(II) supply those electrons. Balanced net: C2H3NO3 + 2 Fe + 4 H+ -> C2H5NO2 + H2O + 2 Fe(2+).
reactions.reasoning: Metallic-iron-promoted amino-acid formation with hydroxylamine is supported by Muchowska et al. (2019), including the mild 343 K temperature. The explicit oxime edge represents the reduction component of that combined chemistry. Unlike the unbalanced shorthand in the supplied review, this reaction includes the necessary iron and proton consumption. Fe(II) abundance alone does not establish reducing capacity. Iron accessibility, competing corrosion, hydroxylamine supply, and mixture compatibility remain constraints; ammonia-only reductive amination is not inferred from this evidence.

pathways.name: Supplied formaldehyde through ammonia-first Strecker hydrolysis
pathways.description: Boundary-supplied formaldehyde, HCN, and ammonia form aminoacetonitrile, followed by staged acidic hydration and amide hydrolysis. This is the principal conventional synthesis route.

pathways.name: Supplied formaldehyde through a cyanohydrin reservoir and hydrolysis
pathways.description: Formaldehyde is initially captured as glycolonitrile, then exchanges into aminoacetonitrile under ammonia-rich conditions before hydrolysis. This is a reservoir-resolved Strecker variant, not an independent reaction family.

pathways.name: Supplied formaldehyde through Strecker formation and hydantoin processing
pathways.description: Ammonia-first aminonitrile formation is followed by carbonate-dependent hydantoin capture, alkaline ring opening, and decarbamoylation. Natural carbonate concentration and productive severe hydrolysis remain conditional.

pathways.name: Supplied formaldehyde through cyanohydrin and hydantoin reservoirs
pathways.description: The glycolonitrile pool feeds aminoacetonitrile, which enters the hydantoin branch. Both reservoir exchanges require measured productive conversion; neither is assumed to improve yield or stability.

pathways.name: HCN photoreduction followed by ammonia-first Strecker hydrolysis
pathways.description: Cyanosulfidic photochemistry supplies formaldehyde, which is intercepted in an ammonia-rich compartment and converted through aminoacetonitrile and glycinamide to glycine. Additional HCN remains available for carbon-chain assembly.

pathways.name: HCN photoreduction followed by cyanohydrin capture and hydrolysis
pathways.description: Photogenerated formaldehyde enters the glycolonitrile reservoir before ammonia-driven exchange and conventional hydrolysis. Product interception must outcompete continued photochemistry and volatile loss.

pathways.name: HCN photoreduction followed by Strecker and hydantoin conversion
pathways.description: Photochemical formaldehyde production feeds ammonia-first aminonitrile synthesis and the hydantoin branch. This combines a literature-supported reaction family with explicitly conditional carbonate capture and hydrothermal processing.

pathways.name: HCN photoreduction through cyanohydrin and hydantoin reservoirs
pathways.description: The photochemical carbon supply passes through glycolonitrile, aminoacetonitrile, hydantoin, and hydantoic acid. This is the most operationally demanding Strecker-family variant and is not presented as an independently validated integrated synthesis.

pathways.name: Supplied glyoxylic acid through oxime formation and iron reduction
pathways.description: Boundary-supplied glyoxylic acid reacts with hydroxylamine and is reduced with explicitly consumed metallic iron. This pathway does not assume that either precursor's environmental supply has been solved.

pathways.name: Conditional CO2 photoredox supply followed by oxime reduction
pathways.description: CO2/sulfite photochemistry is proposed to supply an analytically verified, accessible glyoxylic-acid pool, followed by hydroxylamine condensation and iron reduction. The photochemical supply and transfer remain conditional rather than a claimed selective or integrated demonstration.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The strongest pathway: conventional Strecker formation followed by nitrile hydration and amide hydrolysis provides a chemically valid route to glycine. Aminoacetonitrile and glycinamide are correctly identified, and all three reactions conserve atoms and charge. Patel et al. (2015, DOI: 10.1038/nchem.2202) supports the related aminonitrile chemistry, but unspecified aqueous surface conditions do not establish useful hydrolysis rates. Separating ammonia-rich formation from acidic hydrolysis is appropriate.
suggestions: Provide pH, temperature and residence time for both hydrolysis stages; distinguish literature measurements from proposed conditions.
Specify the initial ammonia inventory, reagent concentrations and transfer into the acidic compartment, including dilution and competing aminonitrile reactions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Formaldehyde cyanohydrin formation is well-founded, and the downstream hydrolysis chemistry is valid. Conversion of the glycolonitrile reservoir into aminoacetonitrile is plausible through reversible cyanohydrin dissociation and subsequent imine/cyanide chemistry, rather than necessarily direct displacement of hydroxyl by ammonia. Its productive extent depends on ammonia activity, pH and competing reactions. The supplied record does not establish those operating conditions or hydrolysis times.
suggestions: Document the mechanism, equilibrium behavior and yield of rxn_004 at the intended ammonia concentration and pH.
Specify hydrolysis conditions and demonstrate that reservoir release and aminonitrile conversion outpace degradation or polymerization.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The Bucherer-Bergs/hydantoin sequence is chemically recognizable, and all listed transformations are balanced. Aminoacetonitrile plus CO2 is a defensible net representation of carbonate-dependent hydantoin formation, but the carbonate/ammonia speciation and productive conditions require documentation. Hydantoin ring opening does not by itself establish complete conversion to glycine: cleavage of the remaining carbamoyl group can require substantially more severe conditions. Surface-to-hydrothermal transfer is possible but not physically specified.
suggestions: Add primary experimental support and operating conditions for aminoacetonitrile-to-hydantoin conversion.
Specify a physically plausible transport mechanism and temperature, pressure, alkalinity and residence time for hydrothermal processing.
Quantify hydantoic acid conversion to glycine separately from hydantoin ring opening, including competing thermal loss.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a plausible reservoir-mediated variant of the hydantoin family, not an independently established glycine mechanism. There are no conservation violations. The principal uncertainties are productive ammonia-driven release from glycolonitrile, carbonate-dependent hydantoin capture, and sufficiently complete carbamoyl hydrolysis. Hydantoic acid accumulation is not equivalent to glycine production. The proposed compartments avoid obvious simultaneous pH incompatibilities, but transport and operating windows remain unspecified.
suggestions: Establish glycolonitrile-to-aminoacetonitrile conversion under conditions compatible with subsequent carbonate capture.
Provide hydantoin and hydantoic acid conversion data, emphasizing the rate-limiting decarbamoylation step.
Describe transfer, dilution and intermediate survival between surface formation and hydrothermal processing.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The downstream Strecker/hydrolysis route is strong. Cyanosulfidic literature, including Patel et al. (2015), supports the upstream chemical family, but rxn_001 is a lumped net photoreduction rather than a sufficiently specified implementation. Its inferred coefficients are chemically reasonable; the factor of eight follows from representing elemental sulfur as S8. Recoverable formaldehyde yield, sulfur speciation and the required photochemical catalytic system are not established by the supplied summary.
suggestions: Specify UV wavelength, photon exposure, pH and any required copper-cyanide or alternative demonstrated photoredox system.
Demonstrate delivery of a usable formaldehyde/ammonia pool and allocate additional HCN for Strecker capture.
Define transfer out of irradiation and the subsequent acidic hydrolysis conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The pathway is connected and atom-balanced, with valid downstream glycine-forming chemistry. Glycolonitrile can plausibly trap photochemically supplied formaldehyde, but a reservoir is productive only if it subsequently releases material into aminoacetonitrile formation. Both the usable output of rxn_001 and the extent of rxn_004 require quantitative justification. Separating irradiation, ammonia-rich processing and acidic hydrolysis is chemically sensible.
suggestions: Measure or substantiate photochemical formaldehyde capture into glycolonitrile under the intended cyanide and sulfur conditions.
Specify ammonia-driven reservoir exchange and protect the resulting aminonitrile from continued irradiation.
Provide hydrolysis times and account for dilution and side-product carryover during compartment transfer.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Each module has a plausible chemical basis, and no reaction violates conservation. However, support for cyanosulfidic precursor formation does not establish the subsequent carbonate capture and complete hydantoin-to-glycine conversion. The conditional status of this extension is appropriately acknowledged. Confidence is limited by unspecified photochemical requirements, hydrothermal transfer, and the severity and selectivity of hydantoic acid decarbamoylation—not by the number or order of environments.
suggestions: Provide reaction-specific evidence for photochemical feed production and carbonate-dependent hydantoin formation.
Define transport and any necessary separation from sulfur-containing photochemical residues.
Establish a hydrothermal window giving substantial glycine recovery rather than only ring opening or decomposition.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway combines the uncertain productive output of photoreduction, ammonia-driven cyanohydrin exchange and conditional hydantoin processing. Its equations are balanced and its intermediate identities are coherent, but continuity of productive material flow is not yet established. In particular, capture into glycolonitrile or hydantoin cannot be treated as evidence of final glycine yield without demonstrating release and complete hydrolysis.
suggestions: Substantiate flux through both reservoir-release steps using realistic concentrations and residence times.
Provide primary citations and specific conditions for the hydantoin module.
Document intermediate survival, transport and final glycine selectivity under the proposed hydrothermal conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Oxime formation followed by iron-driven reduction is a chemically credible glycine route. Explicitly consuming metallic iron correctly supplies the four-electron reduction and improves upon the incomplete reductant bookkeeping in the supplied review. Muchowska et al. (2019, DOI: 10.1038/s41586-019-1151-1) supports related iron/hydroxylamine amino-acid formation. A heated surface compartment could reproduce relevant aqueous conditions, but the surface label alone does not establish equivalence to the reported 70 C chemistry.
suggestions: Encode rxn_012 explicitly as oxime + 2 Fe + 4 H+ -> glycine + 2 Fe2+ + H2O.
Specify temperature, proton activity, iron loading and surface area, and any requirement for initially added Fe2+.
Document glycine selectivity relative to hydrogen evolution, iron passivation and competing reduction of hydroxylamine.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The unchecked photoredox equation is manually balanceable: 2 CO2 + 2 SO3^2- + H2O -> C2H2O3 + 2 SO4^2-. It is therefore not a conservation violation. Liu et al. (2021, DOI: 10.1038/s41557-021-00789-w) supports CO2/sulfite photoredox chemistry, but the productive yield and transferability of a glyoxylic-acid-equivalent pool require reaction-specific evidence. Downstream oxime formation and iron reduction are plausible; compatibility with residual sulfite and other photoproducts remains unresolved.
suggestions: Use parseable sulfite/sulfate charge representations and record the balanced coefficients for rxn_010.
Specify irradiation conditions and quantify free, hydrated and sulfite-bound glyoxylate-equivalent material available for oxime formation.
Demonstrate a physically justified transfer or conditioning step that preserves the carbonyl-equivalent pool and permits selective iron reduction.

evaluation.network_feedback: Not approved at the network threshold of 0.90. Structural validity is high: the 21 molecule nodes and 12 reaction nodes form a connected network, IDs are consistent, and there are no established atom/charge conservation violations. The reported coefficients for rxn_001 and rxn_012 are reasonable, and manual balancing resolves the parser-limited rxn_010. Neutral acid-reference formulas are acceptable bookkeeping and are not themselves conservation errors. The conventional Strecker/glycinamide core genuinely provides a valid route to glycine; the oxime/iron family is also credible. Hydantoin processing and transferable photochemical glyoxylate supply remain less well substantiated. Explicit external feedstocks are accepted, and neither pathway counts, hub counts nor compartment order affect this assessment. Separating incompatible chemical conditions is appropriate, but the supplied reaction summaries omit the numerical operating windows and detailed reaction records referenced by the strategy. Important outstanding requirements include hydrolysis kinetics, photochemical catalyst and irradiation specifications, carbonate-dependent capture conditions, complete hydantoic acid conversion, and physical transfer/recovery justification. Literature alignment is strongest at the chemical-family level through Patel, Muchowska and Liu; reaction-level citations and experimental conditions are missing from the supplied network records. Rejecting the review's questionable mechanistic assignments and not counting glyoxylic-acid hydration as synthesis are chemically justified. Listed problematic reactions identify conditional chemistry or implementation/evidence gaps, not conservation failures. The overall score evaluates the complete network without treating its ten graph-distinct pathways as ten independently demonstrated mechanisms.
